title: GLP-1 Medications for Addiction: What the Research Shows
description: Ozempic, Wegovy, and other GLP-1 drugs are showing surprising effects on addiction. Here's what the latest research reveals about semaglutide for alcohol, nicotine, and substance use disorders.
author: HeyPsych Editorial Team

content.text: GLP-1 receptor agonists like semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) were developed for diabetes and weight loss. But patients and researchers started noticing something unexpected: many people on these medications reported dramatically reduced cravings for alcohol, nicotine, and other substances.
What Are GLP-1 Medications?

GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) receptor agonists mimic a natural hormone that regulates blood sugar and appetite. Originally approved for type 2 diabetes, they've become widely prescribed for weight loss under brand names like Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound.
These medications work on the brain's reward system—the same pathways involved in addiction. This overlap may explain their unexpected effects on substance use.
The Research: What Studies Show
A 2023 study in Nature Medicine found that patients on semaglutide had a 50-56% lower risk of alcohol use disorder diagnosis compared to those on other obesity medications.
Multiple lines of evidence support the addiction-reducing effects:

items: Animal studies show GLP-1 agonists reduce alcohol consumption by 40-50%
Patient surveys report reduced interest in drinking, even among non-problematic drinkers
Retrospective analyses of medical records show lower rates of substance use diagnoses
Brain imaging studies reveal reduced reward response to alcohol cues

content.text: How GLP-1 Drugs May Reduce Addiction

The brain's reward system relies heavily on dopamine. Addictive substances hijack this system, creating powerful cravings. GLP-1 receptors are found throughout reward-related brain regions, including the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and nucleus accumbens.
Researchers believe GLP-1 medications may reduce addiction through several mechanisms:

items: Modulating dopamine release in reward pathways
Reducing the 'wanting' component of addiction without affecting 'liking'
Decreasing impulsivity through prefrontal cortex effects
Altering gut-brain signaling that influences cravings

content.text: Which Substances Are Affected?
Alcohol

The strongest evidence exists for alcohol. Multiple studies show reduced drinking, fewer binge episodes, and decreased cravings. Some patients report alcohol becoming 'uninteresting' rather than requiring willpower to avoid.
Nicotine
Early research and patient reports suggest reduced cigarette cravings. A 2024 clinical trial is specifically testing semaglutide for smoking cessation.
Opioids and Stimulants
Animal studies show promise, but human data is limited. Several clinical trials are underway testing GLP-1 drugs for opioid and cocaine use disorders.
Important Caveats
GLP-1 medications are not FDA-approved for addiction treatment. Using them for this purpose is off-label and should only be done under medical supervision.
Key limitations of current research:

items: Most studies are retrospective or observational, not randomized controlled trials
Long-term effects on addiction are unknown
Side effects (nausea, vomiting, potential thyroid risks) require careful consideration
Cost and access remain significant barriers ($1,000+/month without insurance)

content.text: Current Clinical Trials
As of 2024, multiple clinical trials are investigating GLP-1 medications for addiction:

items: Semaglutide for Alcohol Use Disorder (University of North Carolina)
Tirzepatide for Cocaine Use Disorder (Mount Sinai)

content.text: What This Means for Treatment

If ongoing trials confirm these effects, GLP-1 medications could become a valuable addition to addiction treatment—particularly for patients with both obesity and substance use disorders. However, they're unlikely to replace behavioral therapies and existing medications like naltrexone.
These drugs won't be a magic bullet, but they could be another tool in the toolbox for people struggling with addiction.
content.citation: Dr. Lorenzo Leggio, NIH addiction researcher

content.text: The Bottom Line

The emerging research on GLP-1 medications for addiction is genuinely exciting. These drugs appear to reduce cravings and consumption across multiple substances by targeting the brain's reward system. However, we're still in early days—controlled clinical trials are needed before these medications can be recommended for addiction treatment.

If you're currently taking a GLP-1 medication and have noticed changes in your substance use, discuss this with your healthcare provider. And if you're struggling with addiction, evidence-based treatments are available now—don't wait for future research to seek help.
